title: Coding Basics · Episode 1
chapters: Babbage, Lovelace and the first computer design
How computers store letters and emoji
How files get squeezed: the art of compression

units.t: Coding Basics. Episode one.
In this episode: Babbage, Lovelace and the first computer design, What code really is, How computers store letters and emoji and How files get squeezed: the art of compression.
Part one. Babbage, Lovelace and the first computer design.
In the 1830s, long before electricity was in homes, a cranky English mathematician designed a programmable computer made of brass gears.
A young countess saw what it could become.
Tables full of mistakes.
In the early 1800s, sailors, engineers, astronomers and bankers relied on thick books of mathematical tables: logarithms, tide times, star positions and interest calculations.
People called 'computers', a job title long before it meant a machine, worked them out, and typesetters copied them by hand.
Errors crept in at every stage, and a wrong digit in a navigation table could put a ship on the rocks.
Charles Babbage, a brilliant and famously argumentative English mathematician, was frustrated.
By his own later story, while checking tables with his friend John Herschel, he wished steam could do the calculations.
The Difference Engine.
In the 1820s, Babbage designed a machine to produce tables mechanically.
It used the method of differences, which turns many formulas into repeated addition, something gears can do reliably.
It would even print results, removing copying errors.
The British government funded it, and Babbage hired a skilled engineer, Joseph Clement.
A small working section impressed visitors.
But the machine needed thousands of precisely machined parts, and disputes over money and tool ownership plagued the project.
Work stopped in the early 1830s.
By then Babbage had become distracted by a far more ambitious idea.
The Analytical Engine.
The Analytical Engine was designed to carry out any calculation.
It had a 'store' for holding numbers and a 'mill' for arithmetic, roughly what we now call memory and a processor.
Instructions came on punched cards, an idea borrowed from the Jacquard loom, which wove complex patterns into silk.
Crucially, the machine could choose what to do next based on its own results, and repeat sets of instructions.
Those features mean it could follow programs, the defining trait of a computer.
Babbage refined the design for decades, but the Analytical Engine was never built.
Ada Lovelace's notes.
Augusta Ada Byron was born in 1815, the only legitimate child of the poet Lord Byron, who left when she was a baby.
Her mother ensured she had an unusually strong education in mathematics and science.
Around seventeen, Ada met Babbage and saw part of the Difference Engine.
She was captivated, and later, as Countess of Lovelace, kept up a lively correspondence with him.
In 1842, Luigi Menabrea published a paper describing the Analytical Engine.
Lovelace translated it and added notes about three times longer.
In Note G she set out a method to calculate the Bernoulli numbers, often called the first published computer program.
Historians debate how much was Babbage's, but her notes were the clearest account of the time.
Beyond numbers.
Babbage mostly saw a powerful calculator.
Lovelace saw more: the engine could manipulate any symbols whose relationships follow rules.
If musical sounds could be captured that way, she speculated, it might compose music.
She also cautioned that it could only do what it was instructed to do.
In 1950, Alan Turing called this 'Lady Lovelace's objection'.
She died in 1852, aged 36.
Was Babbage too far ahead of his time, or were his designs flawed?
The Science Museum in London built his Difference Engine No. 2 from his drawings, using tolerances achievable in his era.
Finished in 1991, it worked.
A programming language, Ada, is named for her.
The key idea: Babbage wanted machines to calculate error-free mathematical tables, because human 'computers' and typesetters let mistakes creep in.
Part two. What code really is.
Every app on your phone is just a very long, very precise recipe.
Once you see the five ingredients, software stops being magic.
A recipe for machines.
At its heart, code is a list of instructions written for a computer.
Think of a recipe: preheat the oven, mix the flour and eggs, bake for 30 minutes.
A computer follows instructions the same way, one step at a time, in order.
The difference is that a computer has no common sense.
A human cook will notice if the recipe forgets to say 'crack the eggs first'.
A computer will happily throw the eggs in whole.
Programming is the craft of writing instructions so clear that something with zero judgement can still get them right.
The first programmer.
The idea is older than electronic computers.
In 1843 the English mathematician Ada Lovelace published notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, a mechanical computer that was designed but never completed.
Her notes included a step-by-step method for calculating a sequence called the Bernoulli numbers, often described as the first published computer program.
She also saw that such a machine might one day work with music or symbols, not just numbers.
Today a modern car runs on millions of lines of code, but each line is still an instruction in the spirit of hers.
Variables and conditions.
Programs remember things with variables.
Picture a pantry of labelled jars: 'sugar', 'flour', 'eggs left'.
A variable is a labelled jar holding a value, such as a number, a word or a list.
A banking app might keep a variable called balance holding 250.
Buy a coffee and the program takes the value out, subtracts 5, and puts 245 back in the same jar.
Recipes also contain decisions: if the cake is still wet in the middle, bake it five more minutes.
Code does this with conditions, usually written with 'if'.
A thermostat program might say: if the temperature is above 24 degrees, turn on cooling; otherwise, leave it off.
Rejecting a wrong password is a condition at work.
Loops and functions.
Nobody writes a recipe that says 'stir, stir, stir' 200 times; they write 'stir until smooth'.
That is a loop: repeating a block of steps a set number of times, or until a condition is met.
A music app loops through every song in a playlist.
Computers never get bored or tired.
Many recipe books have a basic white sauce on one page, and other recipes just say 'make one quantity of white sauce'.
In code that is a function: a named bundle of instructions you can call whenever needed, taking inputs and handing back a result.
A shopping app might have one that takes a price and a postcode and returns the delivery cost.
Write it once, test it once, use it everywhere.
Combine and try it.
These few building blocks make everything from calculators to video games.
In a step counter, a variable stores today's steps.
A loop keeps checking the motion sensor.
A condition asks whether the phone moved in a walking pattern, and if so adds one.
A function turns steps into kilometres, and another condition checks whether you've hit your goal.
Large programs work the same way, organised into layers so teams can each work on one part.
To try it yourself, Scratch is a free tool from MIT where you snap together coloured blocks labelled 'repeat', 'if' and 'set variable' and watch a cartoon character obey.
Next time you use an app, try spotting where it remembers, decides or repeats.
The key idea: Code is a set of precise instructions that a computer follows exactly, step by step.
Part three. How computers store letters and emoji.
Computers only understand numbers.
So how does a letter, a Chinese character or a laughing-crying face survive the trip from your phone to someone else's?
Every letter is a number.
Inside a computer there are no letters, only binary numbers.
To store text, everyone must agree on a table mapping each character to a number.
Send 65 and a receiving computer using the same table shows a capital A. Early computers each had their own tables, so text from one machine could turn to gibberish on another.
In 1963 American standards bodies published the first version of ASCII, the American Standard Code for Information Interchange, refined over the following years.
It used 7 bits, allowing 128 codes: English letters in upper and lower case, digits, punctuation and control codes, such as a 'bell' code that rang a bell on teleprinters.
ASCII was a huge success, but it was designed for English and left out most of the world's writing.
Babel on the screen.
Computers usually store data in bytes of eight bits, which hold 256 values, so many systems used the spare 128 slots for accented letters, symbols or other alphabets.
But different countries and companies filled the slots differently.
Greek, Russian, Hebrew and Western European text each had their own versions, and Chinese and Japanese, with thousands of characters, needed more complex schemes.
Open a document using the wrong table and the numbers came out as the wrong characters.
Japanese users had a word for the jumble: mojibake, roughly 'character transformation'.
Anyone who has seen an apostrophe turn into a string like â€™ on a web page has met the same problem.
One code for all.
In the late 1980s, engineers including Joe Becker of Xerox and Lee Collins and Mark Davis of Apple began working on a universal solution.
The Unicode Consortium was founded in 1991 and published the first version of the standard that year.
Its goal: one number, called a code point, for every character in every writing system, past and present.
Capital A is still 65, for compatibility with ASCII, and is written in Unicode as U+0041.
Unicode now covers well over 150,000 characters across more than 160 scripts, including Arabic, Devanagari, Cherokee, Egyptian hieroglyphs and cuneiform.
New characters are added through a formal proposal process, and the standard is updated roughly once a year.
A design on a placemat.
Giving characters numbers is only half the job; you also need a way to store them as bytes.
One evening in September 1992, computer scientists Ken Thompson and Rob Pike, then at Bell Labs, sketched a scheme on a placemat in a New Jersey diner.
It became UTF-8.
Its elegance is that ordinary English text is stored exactly as in ASCII, one byte per character, so old files and programs keep working.
Other characters use two, three or four bytes, with bit patterns that clearly mark where each character starts, so software never mistakes part of one character for another.
UTF-8 spread steadily, and today the great majority of web pages use it, a quiet but enormous victory for compatibility.
Emoji arrive.
Emoji come from Japan: e means picture and moji means character.
The resemblance to 'emotion' is a coincidence.

In 1999 Shigetaka Kurita created 176 simple 12 by 12 pixel designs for NTT Docomo's mobile internet service, now held by New York's Museum of Modern Art, though another carrier had offered picture symbols slightly earlier.
Each carrier used its own codes, so emoji broke between networks.
Pressure from companies including Google and Apple led to emoji joining Unicode in 2010.
Unicode gives each emoji a code point and name, such as U+1F602, 'face with tears of joy', but not the artwork, so Apple, Google and others draw their own.
Skin tones attach as modifiers, and family emoji join several with an invisible zero-width joiner, so one picture can use seven or more code points.
The key idea: Computers store text as numbers using a shared table, and ASCII was the first widely successful one, though only for English.
Part four. How files get squeezed: the art of compression.
A whole CD's worth of music can shrink to about a tenth of its size, so thousands of songs fit on your phone.
Compression works by finding patterns, and by cleverly throwing away what your eyes and ears will not miss.
Making files smaller.
One minute of uncompressed CD-quality stereo audio takes about ten megabytes.
Uncompressed high definition video would need hundreds of megabytes every few seconds, far more than a typical home connection could carry.
Yet you stream films on a train and store thousands of photos on a phone.
The trick is compression: representing the same information, or something close enough, in fewer bits.
Lossless compression shrinks a file so it can be rebuilt perfectly, bit for bit.
Lossy compression goes further by discarding details people are unlikely to notice.
Most media you enjoy relies on clever lossy methods built on top of lossless ideas.
Patterns and short codes.
Picture a clear blue sky, where a row holds a thousand identical blue pixels.
Instead of storing blue a thousand times, store 'blue, repeated 1,000 times'.
This is run length encoding.
A more powerful method from Abraham Lempel and Jacob Ziv in the late 1970s replaces repeated sequences with a short pointer: 'go back this far and copy this many characters'.
Variations power ZIP files, PNG images and web page transfers.
Morse code already used another idea: the common letter E is one dot, while rare Q gets a long pattern.
In 1952, David Huffman, then an MIT student, published a method for building the best such code.
Truly random data cannot be shrunk at all.
How JPEG fools your eyes.
Lossy image compression exploits quirks of human vision.
JPEG, a standard from the early 1990s, first separates brightness from colour.
Our eyes are far more sensitive to brightness differences than colour ones, so JPEG usually stores colour at lower resolution.
Next it splits the image into small blocks, typically eight by eight pixels, and describes each as a mix of smooth patterns, from broad gradients to fine stripes.
The fine, busy patterns matter least to our eyes, so they are rounded off heavily or thrown away.
Lossless coding then packs what remains.
Push the quality setting down and the trick shows: blurry edges, smudged colours and visible square blocks.
How MP3 fools your ears.
Audio formats such as MP3, developed in Germany in the late 1980s and early 1990s, and the later AAC, use psychoacoustics, the science of how we perceive sound.
We cannot hear very high or very low frequencies well, and a loud sound masks quieter sounds at nearby frequencies.
An encoder analyses music in short slices, works out which parts would be masked or inaudible, and spends fewer bits on them or drops them.
The result can be roughly a tenth the size of the original CD audio while sounding very similar to most listeners.
At low bit rates, you may hear swirly, watery artefacts, particularly in cymbals and applause.
Video and lost generations.
Consecutive video frames are usually very similar.
In a newsreader shot, the background barely changes.
Codecs such as H.
265 and AV1 store full keyframes only occasionally, and describe how blocks have moved since an earlier frame, plus small corrections.
When data goes missing, streams turn into smeared blocks because movement is applied to the wrong picture until the next keyframe.
Confetti, rain and fast panning are hard to compress.
Lossy formats also cause generation loss.
Each time you edit and re-save a JPEG, or share a photo through apps that recompress it, more detail is lost.
Keep an original of anything important, and make compressed copies from that master.
The key idea: Compression stores the same information in fewer bits, either perfectly rebuilt, lossless, or close enough, lossy.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What problem was Babbage trying to solve?
Answer. Errors in hand-calculated, hand-copied tables.
Question two. Why must programming instructions be so precise?
Answer. Computers have no judgement to fill the gaps.
Question three. Why did early text often turn to gibberish between computers?
Answer. Each machine used a different character table.
Question four. What is the difference between lossless and lossy compression?
Answer. Lossless rebuilds exactly, lossy discards some detail.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
